After pushing 1M+ tokens through Qwen 3.8 27B, here is my optimal llama.cpp config for 16GB VRAM (73k Context, Agentic Coding)
Tutorial | Guide

Dando seguimiento a mi post anterior sobre cómo tengo montado mi servidor de presupuesto (Intel N100 + RTX 5060 Ti 16GB), varios me preguntaron por una mirada más profunda a mi configuración real de inferencia y al desempeño agentic en el mundo real.

Como muchos de ustedes, estaba refrescando la página esperando descargar Qwen 3.8 27B apenas salió. Después de pasar todo el fin de semana estresándolo con flujos de trabajo de codificación agentic, logré correr un proyecto completo y grande casi todo de forma autónoma (más de 1M de tokens procesados en total, solo 3 prompts).

Aquí va un resumen rápido de la configuración base antes de meternos en los detalles del config y del workflow.

Specs y parámetros rápidos

Modelo: Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q3_K_XL.gguf

Hardware: RTX 5060 Ti (16GB VRAM) + Intel N100 (4C/4T, 16GB RAM)

Ventana de contexto: 73,728 (73k de contexto) corriendo tranqui en 16GB de VRAM.

Cuantización de KV Cache: q4_1 para el contexto principal

Decodificación especulativa: MTP nativa activada (spec-type = draft-mtp, n-max = 2)

Sampling: temp = 0.65, top_p = 0.95, top_k = 20, min_p = 0.05

El experimento: armar una API completa con 3 prompts

En vez de correr benchmarks sintéticos, metí esta configuración por una cadena real de ingeniería de software: construyendo una REST API no oficial y un servidor MCP para un foro vBulletin heredado.

Prompt 1 (Arquitectura del sitio y análisis): Pedí al modelo que mapee el sitio objetivo. Generó una especificación en Markdown impecable de ~1,500 líneas que cubría análisis estructural, nodos HTML rescatables, payloads JSON esperados, selección de stack, lógica de paginación, autenticación de sesión y endpoints de búsqueda—mucho más a fondo de lo que yo habría escrito a mano.

Prompt 2 (Arquitectura de desarrollo): Usando la spec como única fuente de verdad, diseñó un plan de implementación modular de NestJS dividido en 9 fases de ejecució<windows-path>"fit" para evitar que capas se carguen en la CPU por un error de cálculo automático
fit                 = off
ctx-size            = 73728
context-shift       = 1

# MTP nativa del modelo (Decodificación especulativa)
spec-type           = ngram-mod,draft-mtp
spec-draft-n-max    = 2

# Cuantización de KV (q4_1 nos permite meter contexto de 73k en 16GB de VRAM)
cache-type-k        = q4_1
cache-type-v        = q4_1

# Parámetros de presupuesto de pensamiento / razonamiento
chat-template-kwargs = {"preserve_thinking": true, "reasoning_effort":"medium"}
reasoning-budget    = 5000

# Batches más chicos para evitar picos de VRAM durante prefills masivos
batch-size          = 1024
ubatch-size         = 512

# Ajustes oficiales / recomendados del sampler de cuantización
temp                = 0.65
top-p               = 0.95
top-k               = 15
min-p               = 0.05

There you go, this is my config. I've run a bunch of tests at different power limits and found 230W to be the sweet spot for my ASRock Creator R9700 card. If you get a different brand, you should run your own tests, I have no idea if they use a reference design or they have their own. If you're on Linux, this will work (or rocm-smi, or direct write to sysfs if you wish).

amd-smi set --gpu 0 --power-cap 230

I found no diff in generation speed is the same between 300W and 230W, you get more prefill speed at higher wattage though, so run your own tests and see what you like.

Llama.cpp arguments below. I use it in router mode with this command line. I run it in Kubernetes so just translate to your own setup. I also compile my binary and build my own container image with both Vulkan and ROCm 7.14 support. You'll see below the default device is ROCm0 but I run Qwen on Vulkan1 (yeah, the numbers are different for the 2 devices). For Qwen, Vulkan yields better generation speed and also leaves 1GB extra of VRAM free. ROCm is faster by about 10% on prefill.

If you don't run your own local DNS, set the cors-origin to "*".

llama-server
--mo

There you go, this is my config. I've run a bunch of tests at different power limits and found 230W to be the sweet spot for my ASRock Creator R9700 card. If you get a different brand, you should run your own tests, I have no idea if they use a reference design or they have their own. If you're on Linux, this will work (or rocm-smi, or direct write to sysfs if you wish).

amd-smi set --gpu 0 --power-cap 230

I found no diff in generation speed is the same between 300W and 230W, you get more prefill speed at higher wattage though, so run your own tests and see what you like.

Llama.cpp arguments below. I use it in router mode with this command line. I run it in Kubernetes so just translate to your own setup. I also compile my binary and build my own container image with both Vulkan and ROCm 7.14 support. You'll see below the default device is ROCm0 but I run Qwen on Vulkan1 (yeah, the numbers are different for the 2 devices). For Qwen, Vulkan yields better generation speed and also leaves 1GB extra of VRAM free. ROCm is faster by about 10% on prefill.

If you don't run your own local DNS, set the cors-origin to "*".

llama-server
--models-preset /config/presets.ini
--ui-mcp-proxy
--ui-config-file /config/ui-config.json
--api-key-file /secrets/api-keys.list
--cors-origins "https://host.domain.net"
--host 0.0.0.0
--port "9931"
--log-colors on
--verbosity "4"
--models-max "1"
--threads-http "4"

presets.ini:

[*]
device = ROCm0
load-mode = mmap+mlock
models-max = 1
n-gpu-layers = all
gpu-layers-draft = all
threads = 4
threads-batch = 8
cont-batching = true
jinja = true
flash-attn = on
parallel = 2
ctx-checkpoints = 16
cache-ram = 8192
cache-reuse = 256
kv-unified = true
cache-type-k = q8_0
cache-type-v = q8_0
fit = off
batch-size = 2048
ubatch-size = 1024
reasoning = on
reasoning-preserve = on

[Qwen 3.8 27B]
device = Vulkan1
model = /models/unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-Q6_K.gguf
temp = 0.8
top-p = 0.95
min-p = 0.00
presence-penalty = 0.0
repeat-penalty = 1.0
reasoning = on
spec-type = draft-mtp
spec-draft-type-k = q8_0
spec-draft-type-v = q8_0
spec-draft-n-max = 2
spec-draft-p-min = 0.85
reasoning-preserve = on
chat-template-file = /models/chat-templates/qwen36-chat-template-v22.jinja
ctx-size = 184320

The api-keys.list file is just a bunch of keys generated like this (which I mount from a Kubernetes secret synced from my 1Password Vault). When I assign one (e.g. to OpenWebUI) I add a comment on the line above so it's easy to track - small home setup so I don't care about databases and such)

for i in $(seq 1 20); do echo "sk_$(openssl rand -hex 32)"; done

Anyway, have fun, it's a nice card.

Thank you so much this much details.

I also compile my binary and build my own container image with both Vulkan and ROCm 7.14 support.

Please share the cmake build commands with flags you're using. I remember that compiling for our cards could give extra performance(~10%), many mentioned that here in past.

LightBroom
•
3d ago

Something like this, it auto-detects the card but you can add a target if you want (or you are compiling for a container image), e.g. -DGPU_TARGETS=gfx1201 for the R9700

HIPCXX="$(hipconfig -l)/clang" HIP_PATH="$(hipconfig -R)" \
    cmake -S . -B build \
    -DGGML_HIP=ON \
    -DGGML_HIPBLAS=ON \
    -DGGML_HIP_RCCL=ON \
    -DGGML_HIP_ROCWMMA_FATTN=ON \
    -DGGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON \
    -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON \
    -DGGML_VULKAN=1 \
    -DGGML_VK_ALLOW_GRAPHICS_QUEUE=1 \
    -DGGML_RPC=ON \
